title: Paper 1 Question 4: evaluating a statement
specPoints: Paper 1 Section A: Question 4 (AO4, 20 marks): evaluating a statement about the second part of the source

tips.title: Twenty marks, twenty minutes
tips.body: Question 4 is half of Section A. Give it the time: two or three minutes rereading the named part with the statement in mind, then the answer. Overrunning on Question 2 is how these marks are lost.

tips.title: Judgement, method, reader, reference
tips.body: Every point in an evaluation has four parts: how far the statement holds here; the choice that produces the impression; what the reader is made to feel; a short quotation. Leave any one out and the point drops a level.

tips.title: The overstatement is the hinge
tips.body: really, totally, clearly, always, simply, nothing at all: the statement overstates so that you can measure it. Find the word, and the position writes itself: to a large extent on this claim, much less on that.

tips.title: One however, with its own method
tips.body: A single turn in the argument, carrying a method and a reference of its own, is what the descriptor means by critical. It is worth more than a paragraph of hedging and takes two sentences.

tips.title: On the focus, in the lines
tips.body: The statement names the claims and the question names the lines. A paragraph on something the statement does not claim, or on the first part of the source, cannot reach the top however good it is.

tips.title: End on the extent
tips.body: The question asked to what extent. The last sentence answers it in the statement's own words: right about the pity, wrong about pathetic; unfair in its excess, not in its origin.

why.matters: Evaluation is the skill of holding a claim up against the evidence and saying how far it survives, and it is the one the exam pays most for in the reading section. Question 4 gives a student someone else's confident sentence about a text and twenty marks for testing it: agreeing where the writer's choices support it, resisting where they do not, and saying why in terms of what the reader is made to feel. The same move, taking a statement apart into its claims, finding its overstatement, and weighing each against what is actually there, is the one that reading anything critically requires, and it is the difference between having an opinion and having an argument.

examples.title: A review, and a reply to one
examples.body: A film review says a performance is wooden and the film has no heart. The reader who watches it and can say the performance is stiff in the first act and not after, and that the last scene has plenty of heart if you attend to what is withheld, is doing Question 4: two claims, an overstatement in each, a verdict on each with evidence. Every reply to a review, and every review worth reading, is built that way.

examples.title: Testing what someone tells you happened
examples.body: A witness statement, a complaint, a headline: each is a confident sentence about what a text or an event shows. The person who asks which part is claim, which word overstates, and what in the record actually supports it, is evaluating. Question 4's habit of agreeing with a difference, right about this, wrong about that, and here is why, is how a careful reader handles any account that wants to be believed.

steps.title: Question 4: twenty marks, one statement
steps.body:
Question 4 is half of Section A. It names a part of the source, usually the second part, prints something a student has said about it, and asks: *To what extent do you agree?* Three bullets follow: consider the claim in the statement; evaluate how the writer presents whatever the statement is about; support your response with references to the text. Twenty marks, AO4.

**The June 2024 question.** Lines 18 to the end. The statement: Dick's anger towards Mary is really unfair, and the writer makes it clear that Mary is totally powerless in this relationship. The bullets: consider whether Dick's anger is unfair; evaluate how the writer presents Mary and Dick's relationship; support with references.

**Four levels.** Level 1, 1 to 5: simple, limited evaluation. Level 2, 6 to 10: some evaluation. Level 3, 11 to 15: clear, relevant evaluation. Level 4, 16 to 20: perceptive, detailed evaluation, which the scheme spells out as a convincing and critical response to the focus of the statement, perceptive understanding of the writer's methods, a range of judicious textual detail, and critical, detailed evaluation of the effects on the reader.

**Time.** About twenty minutes: the biggest question in the section deserves the biggest share of the 45.

rows: Perceptive, detailed evaluation: convincing and critical; methods understood; judicious detail
props.title: Twenty marks in four levels

visuals.alt: A table of the four levels of Question 4 with their mark ranges and the words the examiners use

check.prompt: How many marks is Question 4 worth, and what share of Section A is that?
check.solution: Twenty of the forty marks for reading are on Question 4. It deserves about twenty minutes of the forty-five, and students who spend that time on Question 2 leave the biggest marks on the paper unearned.

steps.title: Taking the statement apart
steps.body:
A statement for Question 4 is built to be argued with, and it usually contains two claims and a word that overstates each. June 2024: Dick's anger is *really* unfair; Mary is *totally* powerless. The adverbs are the hinges.

**Two claims, two answers.** Is the anger unfair? Partly: the writer gives it a cause in the flashback to the labour of fetching water, and gives it an excess in the way it is described. Is Mary totally powerless? No: the writer ends the passage with her enjoying his guilt. So the answer is *to a large extent on the first claim and much less on the second*, and that is a position the top level can be built on.

**The trap.** Agreeing with everything, or disagreeing with everything, produces an answer with nothing to weigh. The scheme rewards a convincing and critical response to the focus of the statement, and critical means tested.

boxes.title: Find the claims
boxes.body: Usually two; sometimes one with two parts

boxes.title: Decide on each
boxes.body: Agree, disagree, or partly, with a reason from the text

boxes.title: State the position
boxes.body: How far, and why: the first sentence of the answer

visuals.alt: Four boxes on taking a Question 4 statement apart: find the claims, find the overstatement, decide on each, and state the position

check.prompt: Which reading of the June 2024 statement gives an answer something to weigh?
check.solution: A position that agrees with part and complicates part gives the essay an argument to make: the excess of the anger against its cause, the apparent powerlessness against the guilt that hands Mary power. Agreeing completely, disagreeing completely, or refusing to decide leaves nothing to evaluate.

markScheme.description: The anger is unfair in its excess but has a cause the writer supplies, and Mary is far from totally powerless by the end of the passage

options: The statement is wrong on both counts, because Dick is calm and Mary is in charge of the household from the start
The anger is unfair in its excess but has a cause the writer supplies, and Mary is far from totally powerless by the end of the passage
The statement cannot be judged, because the reader is not told enough about the couple to decide anything
The anger is really unfair and Mary is totally powerless, exactly as the statement says, so the answer agrees completely with both claims and needs no however

steps.title: What the scheme rewarded in June 2024
steps.body:
The indicative content for Question 4 shows how an evaluation is built out of methods. Each bullet pairs a detail with a judgement.

**On the anger.** Dick's reaction is seen through “his face darkened”, a metaphor suggesting the anger changed or possessed him; he looks at her “in incredulous horror” and “as if she had committed a crime”, a simile that makes the anger extreme; his attempts to keep calm are set against the short exclamatory “Listen to me!”; the repeated “wasting it” shows his desperation. And against all that, the flashback to the water-cart, with its shouting and straining, is offered as a justification for the anger.

**On the power.** Mary's desperation for rain, as she “watched the implacable sky for signs of rain”, makes the anger seem more unfair. Then the shift to her perspective, “suffering these hardships”, with the plural implying many problems. And then the turn: Dick's regret is “another of those little scenes that comforted and soothed her”, suggesting she enjoys his guilt, and the list “he apologising, blaming himself, and she forgiving him” implies a routine that shifts the power balance.

The Level 4 example moved through exactly that arc: the simile makes her a criminal and a prisoner, so powerless; however, his being suddenly sorry places her, by the end, in the position of power.

rows: as if she had committed a crime
Extreme; she is made a criminal and a prisoner
A justification: the anger has a cause
A routine that shifts the power

check.prompt: How does the June 2024 Level 4 example use the simile as if she had committed a crime?
check.solution: The example takes the method to a judgement, criminal and prisoner, and then weighs it against a later detail, so the evaluation has two sides and a conclusion. A simile named without a judgement is Question 2 work misplaced.

markScheme.description: It reads the simile as presenting Mary as both a criminal and a prisoner, trapped and powerless, and then sets that against the ending, where his guilt gives her power

options: It uses the simile to prove that Mary really had committed a crime by wasting water on a farm
It notes the simile and moves on to the next quotation without saying anything about it
It reads the simile as presenting Mary as both a criminal and a prisoner, trapped and powerless, and then sets that against the ending, where his guilt gives her power
It says the simile is a good simile because it is vivid and shows how angry Dick is about the water, and then praises the writer for choosing it, which is what the top level wants to see

steps.title: What evaluating means
steps.body:
AO4 is *evaluate texts critically and support this with appropriate textual references*. The top level asks for critical, detailed evaluation of the effects on the reader. Three things, then, in every point.

**A judgement.** Not what the writer does, but how well, how far, or in what way it produces the impression the statement claims. *The writer makes Dick's anger seem excessive by …* is a judgement; *the writer uses a simile* is not.

**A method.** The judgement is earned by naming the choice that produces the effect: metaphor, simile, sentence form, flashback, shift of perspective, listing. Language and structure both count here.

**A reader.** The effect is on the reader: what the reader is made to feel about the character, and whether that supports or undermines the statement.

**Sentence frames that do all three.** *The writer makes the reader feel … through …, which supports the statement because …* and *However, … complicates this, since the reader …*

check.prompt: Which sentence is an evaluation rather than an analysis or a summary?
check.solution: The sentence about the darkened face judges how far the statement holds, names the method, gives the effect on the reader, and weighs it against another detail. Naming two techniques is analysis without a judgement; retelling the quarrel is summary; agreeing because it is unfair is a judgement with no method or reference.

markScheme.description: The writer makes the reader see Dick's anger as excessive by darkening his face like a possession, which supports the statement, although the flashback to the water-cart complicates it by giving the anger a cause

options: I agree with the statement because Dick is very angry and Mary cannot do anything about it, which is unfair on her

The writer uses a metaphor when Dick's face darkens and a simile when he looks at Mary as if she had committed a crime, and both are effective techniques that make the reader picture the scene clearly and feel the tension between the two characters
Dick gets angry with Mary because she has been using the water to cool herself, and he tells her to listen to him and not to waste it

The writer makes the reader see Dick's anger as excessive by darkening his face like a possession, which supports the statement, although the flashback to the water-cart complicates it by giving the anger a cause

steps.title: A Level 4 paragraph on Miss Brill
steps.body: Suppose the statement is: *Miss Brill is a pathetic figure, and the writer makes the reader pity her from the moment the young couple speak.* Focus on the second part of the story, from the couple's arrival to the end. Here is one paragraph built to the top descriptors.

visuals.problem: Build one evaluative paragraph: judgement, method, reader, reference, and a however.

steps.text: Judgement first: the couple's words are built to make the reader wince for her, so the statement holds at that moment.
steps.note: A position on the claim, limited to the moment named.

steps.text: Method and reference: the writer gives the cruelty to dialogue, “Why does she come here at all—who wants her?”, so that the reader hears it as she hears it, and the giggled simile “like a fried whiting” turns the fur she rubbed life into at the start into something ridiculous.
steps.note: Two choices named, a shift of voice and a simile, each with a quotation.

steps.text: Reader: the reader has shared her idea of the play for pages, so the words land on the reader's own pleasure, not only on hers.
steps.note: The effect on the reader, tied to what the structure has done earlier.

steps.text: However: the writer withholds her reaction. She is “still soundlessly singing, still with that trembling smile” as she prepares to listen, and at home the crying is heard, not explained. Pity is complicated by restraint.
steps.note: The other side, with its own method, withholding, and its own reference.

steps.text: Conclusion: the reader is made to pity her, but the writer refuses to make her pathetic; her dignity is kept by what the text will not say, and that is what the statement misses.
steps.note: How far, and why, in one sentence.

rows: The statement holds at the moment the couple speak
Dialogue as a shift of voice; the simile of the fried whiting
The cruelty lands on the pleasure the reader has shared
Her reaction is withheld; the crying is heard, not explained
Pitied, yes; pathetic, no: the restraint keeps her dignity

visuals.alt: A table of the five moves of the worked paragraph on Miss Brill: judgement, methods, reader, however, conclusion

check.prompt: What does the however do for the paragraph?
check.solution: A critical response weighs. The however brings in the restraint of the ending and its method, so that the conclusion can say the reader is made to pity her but not to find her pathetic. Without it the paragraph agrees and stops.

markScheme.description: It tests the statement against a second method, the withholding of her reaction, so the evaluation has two sides and can conclude how far the statement holds

options: It tests the statement against a second method, the withholding of her reaction, so the evaluation has two sides and can conclude how far the statement holds
It shows that the student has changed their mind halfway through the paragraph and now disagrees with the statement completely, which the examiners reward as open-mindedness
It adds a second quotation, which the mark scheme requires before an answer can reach Level 3
It introduces a point about language, because the paragraph had only covered structure so far

steps.title: Methods still count: language and structure together
steps.body:
Question 4 is AO4, but the descriptor asks for perceptive understanding of the writer's methods, and both kinds are welcome. The June 2024 indicative content used metaphor, simile, sentence forms and repetition, and also flashback, a shift of perspective and a list.

**In the second part of Miss Brill.** Language: the couple's “stupid old thing at the end there”, and the simile of the whiting. Structure: the shift of voice to the couple; the withheld reaction; the honey-cake set up and passed by; the return to the box; the last sentence heard rather than explained. And the small choices that carry judgement: the couple are “The hero and heroine, of course, just arrived from his father's yacht”, which is Miss Brill's own romantic casting of the people who are about to wound her, so the writer makes the reader see the blow coming a sentence before she does.

**Use both kinds, and always attach the judgement.** A method in a Question 4 answer is there to earn a verdict on the statement, not to be admired.

rows: Dialogue as a shift of voice
The couple speak; she is seen from outside
The reader is made to wince: pity
The fur like a fried whiting
What she treasured is made ridiculous
The hero and heroine, in her own words
The reader sees the blow coming before she does
The fur back in its box; something crying
The reader supplies the pain she will not name

check.prompt: Why does the sentence casting the couple as the hero and heroine matter for the evaluation?
check.solution: The casting is in her voice, and the reader, a sentence ahead of her, hears it as dramatic irony. That method earns a verdict: the pity is sharpened, and it is directed at a woman still generous in her seeing, which is not the same as pathetic.

markScheme.description: It is her own romantic reading of the people about to wound her, so the reader sees the blow coming a sentence before she does, which sharpens the pity without making her ridiculous

options: It tells the reader that the couple are the main characters of the story and that the ending will be about their love rather than about Miss Brill, so the reader stops attending to her
It is her own romantic reading of the people about to wound her, so the reader sees the blow coming a sentence before she does, which sharpens the pity without making her ridiculous
It is a mistake by the writer, since the couple turn out to be unkind and so cannot be heroes
It shows that Miss Brill is a good judge of people, because the couple are beautifully dressed and in love

steps.title: Two statements to test
steps.body:
For each statement, find the claims and the overstatement, decide on each with a reference, and write the first sentence of the answer: the position.

1. *The young couple are simply cruel, and the writer gives the reader no reason to understand them.*
2. *The ending of Miss Brill is bleak: the writer leaves her with nothing at all.*

For the first, weigh “Ah, be off with you!” and the boy's angry whisper against the giggling. For the second, weigh the box and the crying against what the narration refuses to say. Then write one paragraph on the one you find harder to argue.

boxes.title: Overstatement
boxes.body: simply; no reason; nothing at all

boxes.title: Position
boxes.body: How far, in the first sentence

visuals.alt: Four boxes for testing a Question 4 statement: the claims, the overstatement, references for and against, and the position

check.prompt: The statement says the writer gives the reader no reason to understand the couple. Which detail most complicates that?
check.solution: The boy's whisper is the detail that cuts against the statement, but not because he feels shame about the mockery: he is the one who started it, with the cruellest lines in the exchange. What the whisper shows is his attention turning from mocking Miss Brill to flirting with the girl, which reads the couple's cruelty as careless self-absorption in their own romance rather than a considered cruelty. A critical answer finds the detail that resists the claim and weighs it; the other details support the statement or say nothing about understanding.

markScheme.description: The boy's whisper turns from mocking Miss Brill to flirting with the girl, reading their cruelty as careless self-absorption rather than calculated malice

options: The girl's giggle at the fur, which shows that she finds Miss Brill funny rather than pitiable and that she has not thought about her at all
The description of the couple as beautifully dressed and in love, which makes them attractive
The boy's whisper turns from mocking Miss Brill to flirting with the girl, reading their cruelty as careless self-absorption rather than calculated malice
The fact that they sit where the old couple had been, which shows that they took someone else's seat

steps.title: Convincing and critical: agreeing with a difference
steps.body:
The top descriptor says a convincing and critical response to the focus of the statement. Convincing means the position is argued with methods and references; critical means the statement is tested, not accepted.

**Agree with a difference.** The strongest answers usually agree with the statement's observation and disagree with its explanation, or agree with one claim and complicate the other. *Yes, the reader pities her; no, the writer does not make her pathetic, because …*

**Keep to the focus.** The statement in June 2024 was about anger and power. A paragraph about the heat, however good, was off the focus of the statement and could not reach the top.

**One however, well placed.** A single turn in the argument, with its own method and reference, is worth more than a paragraph of hedging.

**Judicious references.** Short quotations, chosen because they carry a verdict. The scheme's own examples are a few words each.

**End on the extent.** The last sentence says how far, and why, in the terms of the statement.

boxes.body: A position argued with methods and references

boxes.title: Critical

check.prompt: Which opening sentence would the scheme place highest for the statement that Miss Brill is a pathetic figure whom the reader pities?
check.solution: The sentence that agrees with the pity and disagrees with pathetic, and gives the reason, states a critical position on the focus of the statement in one line. The others agree without a method, summarise the story, or list techniques.

markScheme.description: The writer makes the reader pity Miss Brill from the moment the couple speak, but refuses to make her pathetic, because everything that would make her so is withheld

Miss Brill is a story by Katherine Mansfield about a lonely woman who goes to the park every Sunday and is insulted by a young couple
The writer uses lots of techniques, such as dialogue, similes and short sentences, to make the reader feel sorry for Miss Brill and to show what a sad and lonely life she leads
The writer makes the reader pity Miss Brill from the moment the couple speak, but refuses to make her pathetic, because everything that would make her so is withheld

steps.title: Question 4 in one page
steps.body:
Twenty marks for one argued judgement.

- **The shape:** a part of the source, a statement, to what extent do you agree; three bullets: the claim, how the writer presents it, references.
- **Take the statement apart:** two claims, an overstatement in each; decide on each; state the position first.
- **Every point:** a judgement, a method, an effect on the reader, a short reference.
- **Methods are both kinds:** language and structure; the June 2024 scheme used metaphor, simile, sentence forms, repetition, flashback, a shift of perspective and a list.
- **Critical means tested:** one however with its own method and reference; agree with a difference.
- **End on the extent**, in the statement's own terms, and give the question about twenty minutes.

Practised on the second part of *Miss Brill*: the couple's words, the withheld reaction, the box.

rows: How far, in the first sentence
A detail that resists the statement, with its method
The last sentence, in the statement's terms

check.prompt: Which assessment objective does Question 4 assess?
check.solution: AO4: evaluate texts critically and support this with appropriate textual references. It is the only question on either paper that assesses it, and it carries twelve and a half per cent of the whole qualification.

questions.solution: Question 4 is worth 20 marks, half of the forty for Section A and the largest reading question on either paper. About twenty minutes of the forty-five for the section belong to it.

questions.prompt: Which part of the source does Question 4 usually cover?
questions.solution: The question names its lines: in June 2024, from line 18 to the end. Question 3 covers the whole text, Question 2 a printed passage, Question 1 a few lines. Reading the second part again before answering is part of the twenty minutes.

markScheme.description: A named part, usually the second part of the source, from a stated line to the end

The first six lines, as in Question 1

questions.prompt: What are the words at the end of every Question 4 statement, asking for your judgement?
questions.solution: To what extent do you agree? The phrase asks for a position with a degree, not a yes or a no, and the strongest answers give a different degree for each claim in the statement.

accepted: to what extent do you agree

questions.prompt: What does the mark scheme mean by the focus of the statement?
questions.solution: The Level 4 descriptor asks for a convincing and critical response to the focus of the statement. A paragraph on something the statement does not claim, however good, is off the focus and cannot reach the top.

markScheme.description: The claims the statement makes, which the answer must keep to; in June 2024, the anger and the power, not the heat or the farm

options: The student who is quoted in the question, whose opinion the answer must respect
The last word of the statement, which is always the most important
The lines of the source the question names, which the answer must quote from and must not go beyond in any point it makes
The claims the statement makes, which the answer must keep to; in June 2024, the anger and the power, not the heat or the farm

questions.prompt: Which detail did the June 2024 scheme treat as a justification for Dick's anger, cutting against the claim that it was really unfair?
questions.solution: The scheme listed the flashback describing the effort of collecting the water, emphasised through the verbs shouting, yelling and straining, as a justification for the anger. The other details all show the anger's excess; the flashback is the detail that complicates the claim.

markScheme.description: The flashback to the labour of fetching water, with its shouting, yelling and straining

options: The flashback to the labour of fetching water, with its shouting, yelling and straining
The short exclamatory sentence Listen to me!, which showed the anger escalating
The simile of Mary as a criminal, which showed how extreme the anger was
The metaphor of his face darkening, which showed the anger possessing him and changing him into someone she did not know

questions.prompt: How did the June 2024 scheme read the list he apologising, blaming himself, and she forgiving him?
questions.solution: The scheme read the listing as implying a routine that shifts the power balance: the apology and the forgiveness are a pattern, and the pattern gives Mary a position. That is the detail that answered the statement's second claim.

markScheme.description: As a routine between the couple that shifts the power balance towards Mary

options: As proof that Dick is a weak man who cannot control his temper
As a routine between the couple that shifts the power balance towards Mary
As a sign that the couple's marriage is happy and their quarrels are trivial
As the writer's way of showing that Mary is totally powerless

questions.prompt: A student writes: the writer uses a simile, as if she had committed a crime, which is effective. Why does this not evaluate?
questions.solution: Evaluation needs a judgement about how far the statement holds, earned by a method and its effect on the reader. Calling a simile effective is analysis without a verdict; the scheme's own example read the same simile as making Mary a criminal and a prisoner, and weighed that against the ending.

markScheme.description: It names a method and praises it, but gives no judgement on the statement, no effect on the reader, and no reason

options: It uses the word simile, which is not allowed in Question 4 answers because terminology belongs to Question 2 and is penalised elsewhere
It quotes too many words, since references in Question 4 must be single words
It names a method and praises it, but gives no judgement on the statement, no effect on the reader, and no reason
It is about Dick, and the statement was only about Mary

questions.prompt: Put the four moves of a Question 4 answer in order.
questions.solution: Position, points, however, extent. The position comes first so that the examiner reads every point as evidence for an argument; the extent comes last because it is what the question asked.

markScheme.description: the four moves in order

items: State the position: how far you agree, and with which claim
Make each point with a judgement, a method, an effect on the reader and a reference
Turn with a however: a detail that resists the statement, with its own method
End on the extent, in the statement's own terms

questions.prompt: What method does the writer use when the couple's words are given directly in the second part of Miss Brill, so that the reader hears them as she does?
questions.solution: Dialogue, or direct speech: a shift of voice. For the only time the reader hears Miss Brill described from outside, and because the words are given directly the reader hears them as she does. In an evaluation the method earns a verdict: the reader is made to wince for her.

markScheme.description: dialogue

questions.prompt: Why is the withheld reaction in Miss Brill a method that cuts against the word pathetic in the statement?
questions.solution: What would make her pathetic, a scene of her humiliation, is never written. The restraint is a choice, and it earns a verdict: the reader pities her, and the writer keeps her dignity. Naming the withholding as a method is what turns the however into evaluation.

markScheme.description: Because the writer never shows her breaking down: she prepares to listen, passes the baker's, sits in her room, and the crying is heard rather than explained, so her dignity is kept by what the text will not say

options: Because the couple apologise to her before she leaves, so there is nothing to react to
Because the reader is told that she did not hear what the couple said and so was not hurt
Because the writer shows her crying openly in the park in front of the couple, which makes her dignified rather than pathetic since she is not ashamed of her feelings and lets everyone see them

Because the writer never shows her breaking down: she prepares to listen, passes the baker's, sits in her room, and the crying is heard rather than explained, so her dignity is kept by what the text will not say

questions.prompt: A student answers the June 2024 question with two paragraphs on how the writer describes the heat in the first part of the source. What is the problem?
questions.solution: Question 4 is on the part the question names and on the claims the statement makes. The scheme notes that a response only about language outside the given lines is placed in Level 1 or 2, and the focus of the statement, anger and power, is what the top level responds to.

markScheme.description: The question named the second part and a statement about anger and power; the heat in the first part is outside the lines and off the focus, and the scheme places an answer only about language outside the lines in Level 1 or 2

options: The question named the second part and a statement about anger and power; the heat in the first part is outside the lines and off the focus, and the scheme places an answer only about language outside the lines in Level 1 or 2
The problem is only that the student should have used three paragraphs rather than two
The problem is that the heat is a structural feature and Question 4 is about language

There is no problem, because the heat is the cause of the quarrel about the water and so explains the anger, and the examiners expect students to trace an effect back to its cause wherever in the source that cause appears

questions.prompt: Which sentence about the second part of Miss Brill would the scheme call a convincing and critical response?
questions.solution: The convincing sentence argues a position with two methods and two references, and the critical part tests the statement, agreeing with the pity and disagreeing with pathetic. Agreeing flatly, listing methods, or leaving it to the reader are none of them critical.

questions.prompt: A student said: 'Miss Brill is a pathetic figure, and the writer makes the reader pity her from the moment the young couple speak.' Focusing on the second part of the story, from the couple's arrival to the end, write one evaluative paragraph on how far you agree. Include a judgement, at least two methods with references, an effect on the reader, and a however.
questions.solution: The writer makes the reader pity Miss Brill from the moment the couple speak, but refuses to make her pathetic, and the difference is built out of what the text gives and what it withholds. The cruelty is given to dialogue, “Why does she come here at all—who wants her?”, so that the reader, who has shared her idea of the play for pages, hears the words as she hears them, and the giggled simile “like a fried whiting” turns the fur into which she rubbed life in the first paragraph into something ridiculous; the reader is made to wince on her behalf, which is what the statement means by pity. However, the writer withholds her reaction. She is “still soundlessly singing, still with that trembling smile” as she prepares to listen, the walk home is told through the honey-cake she does not buy, and at home the crying is heard rather than shown, so that the scene that would make her pathetic is never written. The effect on the reader is a pity complicated by restraint: the reader supplies the pain the text will not name, and in doing so grants her a dignity the couple denied her. The statement is right about the pity and wrong about the figure, and to that extent I agree with it.

questions.prompt: A student said: 'The ending of Miss Brill is bleak: the writer leaves her with nothing at all.' Focusing on the story from the walk home to the end, write a full Question 4 answer of the length you would write in the exam: a position, three points with methods and references, a however, and a conclusion on the extent.
questions.solution: The ending is bleak, and the writer makes it so by structure rather than by statement; but the claim that she is left with nothing at all is exactly what the writer declines to say, and the difference is where the evaluation lies. The first method is a set-up and a withholding: the reader is told that on her way home she usually buys a slice of honey-cake and that an almond in it makes a great difference, and then that “But to-day she passed the baker's by”; the small ritual, established only to be broken, makes the reader feel the loss without a word of grief, and the effect is bleaker than any description of sadness would be. The second is the shift of place and scale, from the whole company in the park to “her room like a cupboard”: the reader who shared her sense of belonging is shut in with her, and the word cupboard, hers as much as the narrator's, says what the afternoon has done to the size of her life. The third is the return: the fur that came out of its box in the first paragraph, its eyes asking what had been happening to it, goes back in, and when the lid goes on “she thought she heard something crying”. The cyclical structure makes the reader recognise in the fur what has happened to her, and the final sentence, heard rather than explained, is the bleakest thing in the story because the narration will not name it. However, that refusal is also what the statement misses. The writer leaves her with the fur, with the habit of not saying, and with the reader's understanding; she is not shown broken, and the crying is displaced onto the thing she loves, so that her dignity is kept by the very restraint that makes the ending bleak. The ending is bleak to a great extent, and the writer leaves her with less than she had; but not with nothing, and the statement's absolute is the part I would not accept.

questions.prompt: A student's Question 4 answer agrees with every part of the statement and gives six quotations that support it. Where does the scheme place that, and why?
questions.solution: Support without testing is convincing at most. The descriptor pairs convincing with critical, and critical means the statement has been weighed: a however with its own method and reference. Six supporting quotations with no resistance leave the argument one-sided.

markScheme.description: Below the top, because a response that never tests the statement is not critical, however well supported; the top level asks for a convincing and critical response

options: At the top, because six quotations is a range of judicious detail and agreement shows understanding of the statement, and the descriptor asks for nothing more than a convincing response with textual support
At Level 1, because agreeing with the statement is always wrong in Question 4
Below the top, because a response that never tests the statement is not critical, however well supported; the top level asks for a convincing and critical response
Nowhere, because Question 4 answers must disagree with the statement to be marked at all

questions.prompt: Why are structural methods, such as the withheld reaction and the return to the box, as useful in a Question 4 answer as similes and metaphors?
questions.solution: AO4 is evaluation, and any method that produces the impression the statement claims can earn a verdict. The June 2024 indicative content mixed both kinds. What matters is that each method is attached to a judgement about the statement.

markScheme.description: Because the descriptor asks for understanding of the writer's methods without limiting them to language, and the June 2024 scheme itself rewarded a flashback, a shift of perspective and a list alongside metaphor and simile

examTechnique.body:
**Half of Section A on one question.** Twenty marks, about twenty minutes. Reread the named part with the statement in mind before writing.

**Take the statement apart.** Two claims, an overstatement in each. Decide on each and state the position in the first sentence.

**Every point evaluates.** A judgement about the statement, the method that produces the impression, the effect on the reader, a short reference. Language and structure both count; the June 2024 scheme used metaphor, simile, sentence forms, repetition, flashback, a shift of perspective and a list.

**Critical means tested.** One however with its own method and reference. Agree with a difference.

**Stay on the focus and in the lines.** The statement's claims, the named part of the source. End on the extent, in the statement's own terms.
examinerErrors: Agreeing with the whole statement and supporting it with quotations, so that nothing is tested and the response is never critical.
Analysing methods without a judgement: naming a simile and calling it effective.
Writing about the first part of the source, or about something the statement does not claim.
Retelling what happens in the named part instead of evaluating how the writer presents it.
Spending the time on Question 2 and leaving the twenty marks of Question 4 to a few rushed lines.
Ending without saying to what extent, which is the question that was asked.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer opens with a position that has taken the statement apart: right about this claim, less so about that, and why. Each point that follows carries a judgement, a method, an effect on the reader and a short reference chosen because it carries the verdict, and the methods are both kinds, the simile and the sentence form beside the flashback and the withheld reaction. There is one however, placed where a detail resists the statement, with its own method and reference, and the last sentence says to what extent in the statement's own terms. It keeps to the named part and the focus, and it takes about twenty minutes.
